lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: describe the differences between aerobic and anaerobic respiration
know the word equation and the balanced chemical symbol equation for aerobic respiration in living organisms
know the word equation for anaerobic respiration in plants and in animals

primer.text: Cells never sit idle: every process they run, from pumping ions to contracting fibres, has to be paid for in energy. This note walks through how glucose is cashed in — completely, with oxygen, or partially without it — and why the two routes differ so much in their yield and their waste products.

modules.title: Aerobic Respiration
modules.opening: Aerobic respiration is the oxygen-powered route: nutrient molecules are broken down completely inside the mitochondria, transferring a large amount of energy into ATP while carbon dioxide and water leave as the only wastes.
keyPoints: Aerobic means the process needs oxygen and happens in the mitochondria.
Glucose is broken down completely, so the energy yield is large.
The waste products are carbon dioxide and water.
Plant and animal cells alike run this pathway around the clock.

low.restatement: With oxygen present, cells split glucose fully inside mitochondria, giving plenty of ATP plus carbon dioxide and water.
low.analogy: An open fire with plenty of air: complete burning, lots of heat, little left over but ash.
low.examPointer: Quote the definition faithfully: oxygen, nutrient breakdown, ATP release.

medium.restatement: Oxygen lets the enzymes oxidise glucose all the way, so almost every usable joule ends up captured in ATP.
medium.analogy: A full salary versus a part-payment: the aerobic route collects everything the glucose can offer.
medium.examPointer: When asked why the yield is large, answer 'complete breakdown', not merely 'oxygen present'.

modules.title: The Aerobic Equations in Both Forms
modules.opening: The aerobic pathway is written two ways: a word equation naming each substance, and a balanced chemical equation showing exactly one glucose reacting with six oxygen molecules to give six carbon dioxide and six water molecules.
keyPoints: Word form: glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water.
The symbol equation must be balanced for full credit.
One glucose consumes six oxygen molecules.

low.restatement: Learn the word version first, then the balanced symbol one with the sixes attached.
low.analogy: A recipe in plain language versus the exact weighed quantities on a chemist's sheet.
low.examPointer: If the question says 'balanced symbol equation', words alone score nothing.

medium.restatement: Balancing works because each glucose holds six carbons, twelve hydrogens and six oxygens, so six O2, six CO2 and six H2O conserve every atom.
medium.analogy: Atom bookkeeping: nothing may appear or vanish, only be rearranged.
medium.examPointer: Practise writing the symbol version from memory; the balance check earns the marks.

modules.title: Going Without Oxygen in Animals
modules.opening: When muscles demand energy faster than the blood can deliver oxygen, they switch on the oxygen-free pathway: glucose is only partially broken down, a little ATP is transferred, and lactic acid accumulates as the leftover product.
keyPoints: The oxygen-free route needs no oxygen at all.
Glucose breakdown is incomplete, so the ATP yield is small.
Animal muscle cells make lactic acid during vigorous exercise.
Lactic acid lowers tissue pH and can disturb enzymes.
Leftover lactic acid is later oxidised using oxygen.

low.restatement: No oxygen, small payout, lactic acid left behind in the muscles.
low.analogy: Pawning a watch: cash arrives fast, but much of the value stays unclaimed until you buy it back.
low.examPointer: The animal word equation is glucose to lactic acid; no symbol version is required.

medium.restatement: Insufficient oxygen delivery forces the partial route, so energy stays trapped in the lactic acid bonds while the tissue turns acidic.
medium.analogy: A fire starved of air leaves charred half-burnt wood: the fuel was never fully consumed.
medium.examPointer: Link the pH drop to enzyme shape: acidic conditions can denature proteins and slow recovery.

modules.title: Plants, Yeast and the Head-to-Head Comparison
sourceHeadings: Anaerobic respiration in plants and fungi
modules.opening: Plant and yeast cells take the oxygen-free route to a different destination: glucose breaks down into ethanol and carbon dioxide, and in yeast this fermentation is harnessed by bakers, while the comparison table sets the two routes side by side.
keyPoints: Plants and yeast produce ethanol and carbon dioxide without oxygen.
The oxygen-free breakdown in yeast is called fermentation.
Bread-making exploits the carbon dioxide from fermentation.
Aerobic gives a lot of ATP; the oxygen-free route gives a little.
Oxygen use and waste products are the key contrast points.

low.restatement: Without oxygen, plants and yeast make ethanol plus carbon dioxide, and far less ATP.
low.analogy: Two campsites: one runs a full stove (oxygen), the other packs a snack — both feed you, one much better.
low.examPointer: Learn the yeast equation: glucose to ethanol plus carbon dioxide.

medium.restatement: The comparison rests on four axes: oxygen demand, completeness of breakdown, waste products and the amount of ATP transferred.
medium.analogy: Compare runners by distance covered: one finishes the whole race, the other stops halfway.
medium.examPointer: Table questions reward precise pairs: lactic acid for animals, ethanol plus carbon dioxide for plants and yeast.

glossary.definition: The organelles where aerobic respiration releases energy from glucose.
The energy-transfer molecule that cells spend to power their processes.
The partial-breakdown product made by animal cells short of oxygen.
The oxygen-free breakdown of glucose by yeast, harnessed in baking.
